summary: Specifies how the reserved bits in the PIM common header may be used by message types and extends the PIM type space. It updates several PIM-related RFCs.

plainLanguage.summary: PIM (Protocol Independent Multicast) is a family of protocols for sending one message to many receivers. Every PIM version 2 message starts with the same header, and that header holds eight bits that no earlier document explained. RFC 9436 gives those bits a name and rules, and it makes room for 48 new kinds of PIM message.

questions: how many pim message types are there
subtitle: Names the spare bits in the PIM message header and turns three message types into 48.

tldr.problem: All PIM version 2 messages share a common header with eight reserved bits, but no document formally said how each message type may use them, and the type space was running low.
tldr.mechanism: The reserved field is renamed the Flag Bits field and defined per message type. Types 13, 14 and 15 each gain a 4-bit Subtype taken from the flag bits, giving 48 extended types.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 8736, updates six other PIM specifications and updates the IANA PIM Message Types registry.

facts.label: Common header fields
facts.value: 4: PIM Ver, Type, Flag Bits, Checksum

today: RFC 9436 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2023. It obsoletes RFC 8736 and updates RFC 3973, RFC 5015, RFC 5059, RFC 6754, RFC 7761 and RFC 8364. The unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The PIM version 2 messages share a common message header format defined in the PIM Sparse Mode specification, RFC 7761. The common header definition contains eight reserved bits. While all message types use this common header, no document formally specifies that these bits are to be used per message type.

This document updates the definition of the Reserved field and refers to it as the Flag Bits field. It specifies that the flag bits are to be separately used on a per-message-type basis, and it updates the "PIM Message Types" registry to indicate the per-message-type usage.

The originally defined PIM message types were in the range from 0 to 15. Message type 15 had been reserved by RFC 6166 for type space extension. The type space extension in RFC 6166 was made obsolete by RFC 8736, and this document obsoletes RFC 8736 in turn.
sections.plainLanguage: PIM (Protocol Independent Multicast) is a family of protocols for sending one message to many receivers. Every PIM version 2 message starts with the same header, and that header holds eight bits that no earlier document explained. RFC 9436 gives those bits a name and rules, and it makes room for 48 new kinds of PIM message.

sections.title: The PIM Common Header
sections.content:
The common PIM header is defined in Section 4.9 of RFC 7761. This document updates the definition of the Reserved field and refers to it as the Flag Bits field. All other fields remain unchanged.

The header carries four fields. PIM Ver is 4 bits wide and holds the protocol version. Type is 4 bits wide and says which kind of PIM message this is. Flag Bits is 8 bits wide and is the field this document defines. Checksum is 16 bits wide.

The Flag Bits field is defined in Section 4 of this document. The document also gives the bits names so that one bit can be pointed at precisely: the bit immediately following the Type field is bit 7, and the bit immediately in front of the Checksum field is bit 0.
sections.plainLanguage: Every PIM message begins with the same header. It holds the protocol version, the message type, eight flag bits and a checksum. This document gives the eight flag bits a name, the Flag Bits field, and leaves the rest of the header alone.

sections.title: Flag Bits for Each Message Type
sections.content:
Unless otherwise specified, all the flag bits for each PIM type are Unassigned. They MUST be set to zero on transmission, and they MUST be ignored upon receipt. The specification of a new PIM type MUST indicate whether the bits should be treated differently.

Three message types already say something about their bits. Type 4 (Bootstrap) defines flag bit 7 as No-Forward, and the remaining flag bits are unassigned. Type 10 (DF Election) specifies that the four most significant flag bits, bits 4 to 7, are to be used as a subtype, and the remaining flag bits are unassigned. Type 12 (PIM Flooding Mechanism) defines flag bit 7 as No-Forward, and the remaining flag bits are unassigned.

Types 13, 14 and 15 are handled by the type space extension described in Section 5.
sections.plainLanguage: Every flag bit starts out with no meaning. Senders must set them to zero and receivers must ignore them, unless the message type gives them a job. Three types already do: Bootstrap and PIM Flooding Mechanism use one bit each, and DF Election uses four bits as a subtype.

sections.title: Extending the PIM Type Space
sections.content:
This document extends types 13, 14 and 15 such that each becomes 16 new types, resulting in 48 types available for future PIM extensions.

The extension is achieved by defining a Subtype field using the four most significant flag bits, bits 4 to 7. The notation type.subtype is used to reference the new extended types, so 13.0 and 13.1 are two different types that share the same Type value of 13. The remaining four flag bits, bits 0 to 3, are abbreviated FB and are to be defined by each extended type.

Each of the extended types is represented by the eight bits resulting from the concatenation of the Type and Subtype fields. No relationship is expected or implied between extended type messages with a common Type field.
sections.plainLanguage: Three PIM message types are each split into 16, giving 48 types for future extensions. A four-bit Subtype field takes the place of part of the flag bits, and a new type is named by writing both numbers, such as 13.1.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document says that clarifying the use of the flag bits in the common PIM header and extending the PIM type space has no impact on security. There are no changes to the considerations in RFC 7761 and RFC 3973.
sections.plainLanguage: This document says the flag bits and the new message types do not change how PIM is secured. The security rules stay exactly as they are in the PIM specifications.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
This document updates the "PIM Message Types" registry to indicate which flag bits are defined for use by each of the PIM message types, and changes their registration status to Unassigned except where the bits have already been specified. The registration policy remains IETF Review. Assignments to this registry MUST define any non-default usage of the flag bits in addition to the type.

Extended type 15.15 is Reserved for future extensions. Because this document obsoletes RFC 8736, IANA has changed the references to RFC 8736 in the registry to point to this document instead.

The unassigned types above use the extended type notation of type.subtype. Each extended type only has four flag bits available, and new extended message types should be assigned consecutively, starting with 13.0, then 13.1, and so on.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA's list of PIM message types now records which flag bits each type uses, and it says which bits are still free. Type 15.15 is held back for future use. New extended types are handed out in order, starting at 13.0.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: The kind of PIM message. The originally defined types run from 0 to 15.

fields.name: Flag Bits
fields.desc: Formerly the Reserved field. Defined per message type by this document.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: Unchanged from the common header defined in RFC 7761.

viz.caption: THE HEADER FOR AN EXTENDED TYPE

data.title: PIM common header with a Subtype

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: The type part of the extended type. Together with Subtype it names the message.

fields.name: Subtype
fields.desc: Bits 4 to 7. The type part and this field together give the eight bits of an extended type.

fields.name: FB
fields.desc: Bits 0 to 3. Left for each extended type to define.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: Unchanged from the common header defined in RFC 7761.

viz.caption: THE UPDATED PIM MESSAGE TYPES REGISTRY

items.label: Unassigned
items.desc: Flag bits 0-3: Unassigned. Extended types use the type.subtype notation.

items.label: Reserved
items.desc: Flag bits 0-3: Reserved, for future extensions.
